Chapter Ten: The Future of English—Unpredictable, Unstoppable
So, what will English sound like a hundred years from now? Honestly, no one really knows. Maybe it’ll spread even further across the globe... or maybe we’ll see it break off into dozens of fresh, new dialects. Think about it—could technology change the way we speak and write? Or will the classics stick around?
The only thing we can count on is change. And sometimes, that change is impossible to see coming.
Picture this: a linguist stands at the edge of a playground, listening to kids chat and laugh. She’s hearing words and phrases that are completely new to her. Some of these words are borrowed from other languages, while others are just made up on the spot. She knows most of them will fade away, but a handful? They’ll catch on—and become part of English for years, maybe even centuries.
The future of English is going to be shaped by all kinds of forces—technology, migration, politics, culture. As people travel and mix, new forms of English are born, each with their own style and rhythm. In some places, English will merge with local languages, creating entirely new hybrids. Elsewhere, it might stay in the background, just a tool for getting a message across, not really tied to anyone’s identity.
Some people worry about this. They think that as “global English” spreads, local differences will get smoothed out, and the language might lose its charm. But here’s something to remember—English has always been a language of diversity. It’s a patchwork of dialects, accents, and styles. And honestly, the more it’s shared, the more variety we see.
English has never been shy about borrowing, inventing, or adapting. For every new technology, every new experience or way of living, new words pop up. Old words shift and take on new meanings, while some quietly slip away. The language just keeps on growing and changing, surprising us at every turn.
If you love English, that’s part of the magic—right? It’s never finished, never truly fixed. It’s alive, shaped by everyone who speaks it. And as long as people keep talking, English will keep evolving, always finding new ways to capture the endless range of human experience.
